newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: REITH WANTS MODEST DECISION ON LIVING WAGE
Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith says the Government is fully aware of the need to maintain basic wages.
His comment comes as the Industrial Relations Commission prepares to deliver its decision on the ACTU's Living Wage claim, in Sydney this afternoon.
The ACTU wants to maintain wages for workers unable to negotiate an enterprise bargaining agreement.
Mr Reith says the Government wants to see an increase in the award safety net for low income workers, because without it they're likely to miss out.
But the government, employers and the finance sector all say the 20-dollar claim by the ACTU is too high.
BEAZLEY SADDENED TO HEAR ABOUT LAWRENCE
Federal Opposition Leader, Kim Beazley, says many in the A-L-P will be saddened to hear that Carmen Lawrence has been charged with perjury.
But Mr Beazley says the party won't being paying the legal bills of the former Federal Health Minister and West Australian Premier, who's been charged over evidence to the Easton Royal Commission.
Mr Beazley says the loss of Dr Lawrence from the A-L-P's front-bench is a blow, but says it is appropriate for her to stand-down as Shadow Environment Minister.
Mr Beazley says he wishes Doctor Lawrence well.
The Government, meanwhile, is not commenting on the matter.
WHITLAM DEFENDS HIGH COURT
Former Labor Prime Minister Gough Whitlam says hysterical denunciation of the High Court over it's Wik decision on native title is futile and unfair.
Mr Whitlam told university students in Adelaide last night that the courts are simply applying common law principles that Australia inherited from England.
He says legal precedents involving Aboriginal clients cover more than 20 years and the courts must refer to case law.
Mr Whitlam says the High Court justices have come to decisions on the basis of documentary and oral evidence and that's their duty.
CABINET EXPECTED TO DECIDE RADIO AUSTRALIA'S FUTURE
Federal Cabinet is today expected to decide the future of the ABC's international radio service, Radio Australia.

Communications Minister Richard Alston says he's a bit surprised most of the areas apparently threatened for cuts or closure by the ABC Board are the functions identified as ABC priorities by the Mansfield Review.
The ABC's Board has nominated cuts to news and current affairs, local television drama, and regional radio as the possible results of inadequate Government funding.
Senator Alston says the Corporation's funding next financial year remains subject to pre-budget fine-tuning.
